mainTopic: Selling items and animals to idol worshippers: unspecified versus specified requests, רב אשי's rooster questions, רבי מאיר's palm-tree fruit, and local custom on selling small animals.
overview: The גמרא first asks what the משנה means by סתמן (an unspecified request) and פירושן (a specified request). Its first answer is that asking for plain 'wheat' is permitted and asking for 'white wheat' is forbidden. That reading would make a rooster forbidden even when unspecified, so the גמרא changes it. Asking for 'white wheat' is permitted, and only saying outright that it is for עבודה זרה is forbidden, even if the buyer might be bluffing. רב אשי then asks about buyers who seem to be using tricks to get a white rooster, and those questions end in תיקו. Next, רב חסדא struggles with רבי מאיר's ban on selling a 'good palm tree,' and אבימי explains that it means the fruit of a good palm tree. The גמרא then defines the unfamiliar fruit names חצב and נקלבס. A new משנה rules that selling בהמה דקה to non-Jews follows local custom, while בהמה גסה may not be sold anywhere. רב resolves a contradiction from the ban on leaving animals in non-Jewish inns: selling and leaving an animal alone with a non-Jew are allowed or forbidden together in each place.

steps.title: First definition of unspecified and specified
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא argues that the משנה cannot mean the obvious cases. It suggests that סתמן means asking for 'wheat' and פירושן means asking for 'white wheat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: There is no need to say that we sell when the request is truly plain, and no need to say that we do not sell when he openly states it is for idol worship. Rather, 'unspecified' means he says 'wheat,' and 'specified' means he says 'white wheat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proposes a first explanation of what the משנה means by סתמן and פירושן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes the משנה would not bother teaching the two most obvious cases. So it reads the two words as a finer line. Plain 'wheat' is permitted, but 'white wheat' is forbidden because white wheat was used in idol worship.

keyTerms.meaning: An unspecified request: the buyer does not say what the item is for
A specified request: the buyer spells out what he wants

phrases.english: It does not need to be said that when unspecified, we sell,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא פֵּירוּשָׁן צְרִיכָא לְמֵימַר דְּלָא מְזַבְּנִינַן,
phrases.english: and it does not need to be said that when specified, we do not sell,
phrases.notes: 'Specified' here means he openly said it is for idol worship.

phrases.english: rather, 'unspecified' is where he says 'wheat,'
'specified' is where he says 'white' wheat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the discussion of how to define the משנה's terms.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Asking for 'wheat' is unspecified and permitted. Asking for 'white wheat' is specified and forbidden.

steps.title: Problem: a rooster would be forbidden even unspecified
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws a troubling inference: if so, a rooster would be forbidden even when the buyer makes no specific request.
steps.simpleTranslation: By implication, a rooster would not be allowed even when the request is unspecified!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first definition by pointing out an unwanted consequence for the rooster case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists the white rooster separately from 'all other items.' If 'white' already makes other items forbidden, the rooster's separate listing must teach something stricter. That would mean a rooster is forbidden even without any specification. This clashes with the earlier view of רבי זירא, who was more lenient about roosters.

phrases.english: By implication, a rooster,
even unspecified, is also not permitted!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִכְּלָל דְּתַרְנְגוֹל אֲפִילּוּ סְתָמָן נָמֵי לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the definition given in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The definition of סתמן as plain 'wheat' and פירושן as 'white wheat'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'white' is already forbidden for ordinary items, the separate rooster clause would have to forbid even an unspecified request. That contradicts the accepted lenient view about roosters.

steps.title: New definition: white wheat versus 'for idol worship'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא redefines the terms. סתמן means asking for 'white wheat,' and פירושן means saying outright that it is for עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say: actually, 'unspecified' is where he says 'white wheat,' and 'specified' is where he says it is for idol worship.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by shifting both definitions one level up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now asking for white wheat counts as unspecified and is permitted. Only an open statement of idolatrous use is forbidden. This removes the need to read the rooster clause as extra strict.

phrases.english: They say: actually, 'unspecified' is
where he says 'white wheat,'
'specified' is where he says 'for idol worship.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of step 2 by redefining the terms.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Asking for 'white wheat' counts as specified and is forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Asking for 'white wheat' is unspecified and permitted. Only an open statement that it is for idol worship is forbidden.

steps.title: Why the obvious case still needed to be taught
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends the new reading against the original objection that open specification is too obvious to teach. It explains that the buyer might have been bluffing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The specified case was needed. You might have thought this man doesn't really need it for idol worship. Rather, he himself is deeply attached to idol worship and assumes everyone else is too. So he says 'it's for idolatry' just so they will sell to him. The משנה teaches us that it is still forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the משנה had to state that an openly idolatrous request is forbidden, even though that sounds obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 had rejected this reading because it seemed obvious. The answer is that one might suspect the buyer is only saying 'for idolatry' as a sales tactic, thinking it will win over the seller. The משנה (קא משמע לן) teaches that we do not assume he is bluffing, so selling is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: It was needed for him (to teach)
It would enter your mind to say

steps.whatToRemember: Final reading: asking for white wheat is permitted (סתמן). Saying outright that it is for עבודה זרה is forbidden (פירושן), even if he might be bluffing.

phrases.english: And the specified case was needed for him,
since it would enter your mind to say:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי גַּבְרָא לָאו לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה קָא בָּעֵי,
phrases.english: this man does not need it for idol worship,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מֵיבָק הוּא דַּאֲבִיק בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה,
phrases.english: rather, he is deeply attached to idol worship,

phrases.aramaic: וְסָבַר: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא אֲבִיק בֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: and he thinks: just as that man is attached to it,
phrases.notes: 'That man' is a polite way of saying 'I myself.'

phrases.english: everyone else is also attached to it,

phrases.aramaic: אֵימָא הָכִי כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיתְּבוּ לִי,
phrases.english: I'll say this so that they will give it to me,
so it teaches us that it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer of step 3 by removing the objection from step 1 that the specified case is obvious.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the case is not obvious (a חידוש)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A buyer who says 'for idolatry' may just be using it as a tactic to persuade the seller, so selling would be allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: We take his statement at face value, so selling is forbidden.

steps.title: רב אשי: a request for a damaged white rooster
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks about a buyer who asks for a damaged white rooster. May he be sold a whole one, or is the buyer using a trick?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: if someone says 'Who has a damaged white rooster?', may we sell him a whole white rooster? Do we say that since he asked for a damaged one, he doesn't need it for idol worship? Or perhaps he is being sneaky?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי raises a new question about how to read a buyer's request for a damaged white rooster.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A damaged animal would not be offered to an idol, so asking for one suggests an innocent purpose. On the other hand, the buyer may know that no one has a damaged one. He might be asking this way so the seller will offer him a whole one. The question is whether to trust the surface of his words or suspect a trick (איערומי).

phrases.english: Rav Ashi asked:
If one says: 'Who has a damaged white rooster?',

phrases.aramaic: מַהוּ לִמְכּוֹר לוֹ תַּרְנְגוֹל לָבָן שָׁלֵם?
phrases.english: what is the law about selling him a whole white rooster?
Do we say: since he said 'damaged,'
he does not need it for idol worship,
phrases.notes: A damaged animal would not be offered to an idol.

phrases.english: or perhaps he is using a trick?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about the white rooster.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether asking for a damaged white rooster shows an innocent purpose, which would allow selling a whole one, or is a trick, which would forbid it.

steps.title: What if the buyer already took a black or red rooster?
steps.stepSummary: Building on his first question, רב אשי asks a follow-up. A buyer kept calling for a white rooster but accepted a black one or a red one. May we now sell him a white one?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say the buyer who asks for a damaged white rooster is using a trick, what about this case? He called out 'Who has a white rooster?' and was given a black one, which he took, or a red one, which he took. May we sell him a white one? Do we say that since he took a black or red one, he clearly does not need it for עבודה זרה? Or perhaps he is still using a trick?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks a second question that builds on his first. Suppose we treat the 'damaged rooster' buyer as a trickster. What about a buyer who already accepted roosters of other colors?
steps.deeperAnalysis: A white rooster is the one used for idol worship. A buyer who happily takes a black or red rooster seems to show he only wants a chicken for ordinary use. But maybe he took those other colors only to build a cover story, so that he can then get a white one without suspicion.

keyTerms.meaning: If you will say. Introduces a follow-up question that assumes one answer to the first question.
A white rooster, the kind used for idol worship
Or perhaps. Introduces the other side of a question.

phrases.english: If you will say
that this one is using a trick
phrases.notes: This refers back to the buyer from step 5, who asked for a damaged white rooster.

phrases.english: "Who has a white rooster, who has a white rooster?"
and they gave him a black one and he took it
and they gave him a red one and he took it
what is the law about selling him a white one?
Do we say:
since they gave him a black one and he took it,
or a red one and he took it,
he does not want it for idol worship?
Or perhaps he is using a trick?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up question that assumes the stricter answer to רב אשי's first question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does accepting roosters of other colors prove that a buyer who wants a white rooster does not need it for עבודה זרה?

steps.title: The questions stay unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves רב אשי's questions without an answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let it stand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says תיקו. This means the questions stay open with no answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both of רב אשי's questions, the damaged rooster and the black or red rooster, are left undecided. The גמרא found no source that settles whether these buyers are honest or using a trick.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand. The question stays unresolved.

steps.whatToRemember: The rooster questions end in תיקו. We do not know whether these clever-looking buyers may be trusted.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the questions without an answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both questions about tricky rooster buyers remain unresolved.

steps.title: רב חסדא laments how little we understand
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי מאיר's line from the משנה. רב חסדא then tells אבימי that אברהם אבינו's tractate on idol worship had 400 chapters. We have only five, and we do not even understand those.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: רבי מאיר says, even a palm tree and so on. רב חסדא said to אבימי: We have a tradition that the מסכת עבודה זרה of אברהם אבינו had four hundred chapters. We learned only five, and we do not know what we are saying.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new line of the משנה, רבי מאיר's ruling. רב חסדא opens with a complaint that he does not understand it, which sets up the difficulty in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is ruled here. רב חסדא is expressing frustration that even our short five-chapter מסכת is hard to understand. His real difficulty comes in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אַף דֶּקֶל וְכוּ׳.
phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: Even a palm tree, etc.
Rav Chisda said to Avimi:
We have a tradition that the tractate of idol worship of Avraham our father
had four hundred chapters,
and we have learned only five,
and we do not know what we are saying.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: אַף דֶּקֶל וְכוּ׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב חסדא admits he does not understand רבי מאיר's line, which sets up his difficulty.

steps.title: Why would a bad palm tree be allowed?
steps.stepSummary: אבימי asks what is bothering him. רב חסדא explains: רבי מאיר forbids selling a good palm tree, which implies a bad one may be sold. But another משנה forbids selling anything attached to the ground at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is difficult? It is what the משנה teaches: רבי מאיר says it is forbidden to sell even a good palm tree, חצב, and נקלבס to גויים. So only a good palm tree may not be sold, but a bad palm tree may be? Yet we learned that one may not sell them anything attached to the ground!
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי asks what the problem is, and רב חסדא lays out a contradiction between two משניות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'a good palm tree' is forbidden suggests that a bad one is allowed. Yet a separate משנה forbids selling a גוי anything attached to the ground, which would include any living palm tree. So why does רבי מאיר need to say 'good'?

phrases.english: And what is difficult?
phrases.notes: This is אבימי asking. The rest of the step is רב חסדא's answer.

phrases.english: That it teaches: Rabbi Meir says
even a good palm tree, chatzav, and niklaves
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets. The word in square brackets is the corrected spelling.

phrases.english: it is forbidden to sell to non-Jews.
So it is a good palm tree that we may not sell,
but a bad palm tree we may sell?
But didn't we learn: One may not sell them
anything attached to the ground!
phrases.notes: This is a different משנה later in this מסכת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the difficulty behind רב חסדא's complaint
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording implies a bad palm tree may be sold, but another משנה forbids selling anything attached to the ground.

steps.title: It means the fruit of a good palm tree
steps.stepSummary: אבימי answers that 'a good palm tree' means the fruit of a good palm tree, not the tree itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What does 'a good palm tree' mean? The fruit of a good palm tree.
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי resolves the contradiction by reading the משנה as talking about fruit, not the tree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Picked fruit is not attached to the ground, so the other משנה does not apply to it. רבי מאיר is forbidding the fine dates of a good palm, which are used in idol worship. The tree itself is already forbidden as something attached to the ground.

phrases.english: He said to him: What is 'a good palm tree'?
The fruit of a good palm tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב חסדא's difficulty
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'A good palm tree' means the tree itself, which would imply a bad tree may be sold.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means the picked fruit of a good palm tree, so there is no clash with the ban on selling attached things.

steps.title: רב הונא says the same
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא independently explains the phrase the same way: the fruit of a good palm tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so said רב הונא: the fruit of a good palm tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds that רב הונא agrees with אבימי's reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This gives אבימי's answer the backing of a second אמורא. It makes 'fruit of a good palm' the accepted meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: And so said. Shows that another sage agrees.

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר's 'good palm tree' means its picked fruit. The tree itself is already forbidden because it is attached to the ground.

phrases.english: And so said Rav Huna:
The fruit of a good palm tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 10
steps.raayaObject: The reading 'fruit of a good palm tree'

steps.title: What חצב means
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defines חצב as קשבא, a type of date.
steps.simpleTranslation: חצב is קשבא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the unfamiliar words in רבי מאיר's list, starting with חצב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חצב is given a known local name, קשבא, a kind of date. This fits with the previous step, where the list is about fruit.

keyTerms.meaning: A word from the משנה, here explained as a type of date

phrases.english: Chatzav: that is kashba.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to define the next term in the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חצב is קשבא, a type of date.

steps.title: What נקלבס means
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports in the name of רבי חמא בר יוסף that נקלבס means קורייטי.
steps.simpleTranslation: נקלבס: when רב דימי came, he said in the name of רבי חמא בר יוסף that it is קורייטי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a definition of נקלבס, brought by רב דימי from ארץ ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The definition replaces one strange word with another, קורייטי. The next step pokes at exactly that problem.

keyTerms.meaning: A word from the משנה, a kind of fruit
The name for נקלבס used in ארץ ישראל
When he came. Usually means a sage arriving in בבל from ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: Niklaves:
When Rav Dimi came,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בַּר יוֹסֵף: קוּרְיָיטֵי.
phrases.english: he said in the name of Rabbi Chama bar Yosef: koryatei.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר רַבִּי חָמָא בַּר יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the next term in the list

steps.title: אביי: you replaced one unknown word with another
steps.stepSummary: אביי complains to רב דימי that both words are unknown to them, so the definition does not help.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב דימי: We learned נקלבס and do not know what it is. You said קורייטי, and we do not know that either. How have you helped us?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges the usefulness of רב דימי's definition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A definition should explain an unknown word using a known one. Here both words are unfamiliar in בבל, so אביי says nothing was gained.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Dimi:
We learned niklaves and do not know what it is,
and you say koryatei, and we do not know that either.
How have you helped us!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the definition just given
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Explaining one unknown word with another unknown word adds nothing.

steps.title: The new word works in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי answers that in ארץ ישראל people know the word קורייטי. If אביי goes there and asks, they will show him the fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I did help you. When you go there and say נקלבס, they will not know it. Say קורייטי and they will know, and they will show it to you.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי defends his definition by pointing out where it is useful.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קורייטי is the everyday name in ארץ ישראל. So the definition gives a practical way to identify the fruit, even if nobody in בבל recognizes it.
steps.whatToRemember: חצב is a kind of date (קשבא). נקלבס is the fruit known in ארץ ישראל as קורייטי.

phrases.english: He said to him: I did help you,
because when you go there
phrases.notes: "There" means ארץ ישראל, where רב דימי came from.

phrases.english: and say niklaves to them, they will not know it;
say koryatei to them and they will know,
and they will show it to you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The definition is useless because both words are unknown.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word קורייטי is known in ארץ ישראל and lets you identify the fruit there.

steps.title: The משנה: Small animals follow local custom, large animals are forbidden everywhere
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that selling a בהמה דקה to non-Jews follows local custom, but selling a בהמה גסה, calves or foals is forbidden in every place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where people are used to selling small animals to non-Jews, you may sell them. Where people are used to not selling, you may not sell. But everywhere, you may not sell them large animals, calves or foals, whether healthy or injured.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives two rules: small animals depend on what the local people do, and large animals may never be sold to non-Jews.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה draws a sharp line. For a בהמה דקה, each town follows its own practice. For a בהמה גסה, even an injured one, there is one rule for every place: no selling.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה, the base text being studied
Small domestic animal, like sheep or goats
Large domestic animal, like cows or oxen

steps.whatToRemember: Small animals follow local custom. Large animals are forbidden to sell everywhere.

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
A place where they were accustomed to sell
small animals to non-Jews: they may sell,

phrases.aramaic: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ שֶׁלֹּא לִמְכּוֹר — אֵין מוֹכְרִין.
phrases.english: a place where they were accustomed not to sell: they may not sell.
But in every place, they may not sell them
large animals, calves or foals,
whether whole or injured.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ לִמְכּוֹר בְּהֵמָה דַּקָּה לַגּוֹיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה and a new topic after the discussion of fruit names.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling small animals to non-Jews follows local custom; selling large animals, calves and foals is forbidden everywhere, even if injured.

steps.title: Two Sages who allow certain large animals
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה allows selling an injured animal, and בן בתירא allows selling a horse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה allows selling an injured animal, and בן בתירא allows selling a horse.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now brings two Sages who disagree with the strict rule just stated. Each one allows a specific kind of large animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion said even injured large animals are forbidden. רבי יהודה disagrees about injured ones. בן בתירא makes a different exception: a horse.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה's "injured" is the same category the first opinion just said is forbidden ("whole or injured"). He is arguing on that exact point.

phrases.english: רבי יהודה permits an injured one,
and בן בתירא permits a horse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Dissenting opinions on the general ban on large animals from step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה permits selling an injured large animal; בן בתירא permits selling a horse.

steps.title: The גמרא learns that small animals are only a matter of custom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the משנה as saying there is no real איסור on selling small animals, only a מנהג that each place follows.
steps.simpleTranslation: This means there is no prohibition, only a custom. Where the custom is to forbid, they follow that. Where the custom is to permit, they follow that.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a lesson from the משנה's wording: selling small animals is not forbidden in itself. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the משנה makes it depend on the place, the rule must be a מנהג and not an איסור. That means in some places it is fully allowed, and the גמרא is about to ask how that can be.

keyTerms.meaning: That is to say, this shows

phrases.english: GEMARA:
This is to say that there is no prohibition,
it is only a custom that there is,
where the custom is to forbid, they follow it,
where the custom is to permit, they follow it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a conclusion from the first rule in step 16 about small animals.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Selling small animals to non-Jews has no real prohibition; it is only a local custom.

steps.title: A contradiction from the rule against leaving animals in non-Jewish inns
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another משנה: animals may not be left in non-Jewish inns because the non-Jews are suspected of רביעה. That sounds like a real prohibition everywhere.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they contrasted it: One may not leave an animal in non-Jewish inns, because they are suspected of bestiality.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 18. Another משנה forbids even leaving an animal alone with non-Jews, so selling one to them should be forbidden everywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we may not even leave an animal with a non-Jew for a short time, then selling it to him for good should surely be forbidden. This clashes with the idea that small animals are only a custom.

keyTerms.meaning: And they pointed out a contradiction

phrases.english: And they raised a contradiction:
One may not keep an animal
in the inns of non-Jews,
because they are suspected of bestiality.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion of step 18 that selling small animals is only a custom.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 18 that there is no real prohibition on selling small animals.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If leaving an animal alone with a non-Jew is forbidden because of suspected רביעה, selling it to him should be forbidden in every place.

steps.title: רב: The two rules go hand in hand
steps.stepSummary: רב answers that the rules are linked: where selling is allowed, leaving the animal alone is allowed; where leaving it alone is forbidden, selling is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: A place where they allowed selling, they allowed leaving the animal alone with them. A place where they forbade leaving it alone, they forbade selling.
steps.whatsHappening: רב resolves the contradiction by linking the two rules. Each place is treated the same for both selling and leaving an animal alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry about רביעה is not the same everywhere. A place that allows selling must be one where the non-Jews are not suspected, so leaving animals alone there is also fine. Where they are suspected, both are forbidden, so there is no contradiction.
steps.whatToRemember: רב's rule: selling an animal and leaving it alone with a non-Jew rise and fall together in each place.

phrases.english: רב said:
A place where they permitted selling, they permitted leaving it alone,
phrases.notes: "Leaving it alone" means leaving the animal alone with the non-Jew, like in the inn case.

phrases.english: a place where they forbade leaving it alone, they forbade selling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Linking the two rules so both depend on the same local situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ban on leaving animals in inns seemed to apply everywhere, which would forbid selling everywhere too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both rules depend on the place: where selling is allowed, leaving alone is allowed, and where leaving alone is forbidden, selling is forbidden.
